title: Ash-Shakur, the Appreciative
hook: the Appreciative, who rewards the smallest good

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Wadud, the Loving, whose love is shown. Your line was loved. Did you do the deed, and keep quiet about it? Day two hundred fifty-two, the end of a week.

You held a door. You wiped the counter someone else left sticky. You moved the scooter off the sidewalk so the next person with a stroller wouldn't have to. Nobody saw. Nobody said thanks. And a small voice in you said: well, that didn't count. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told a story about a man walking down a road who found a thorny branch lying across it. He moved it out of the way, so it wouldn't hurt anyone. That's the whole deed. And the hadith, in Sahih al-Bukhari, says God thanked him for it, and forgave him. God thanked him. For a branch. Today, the name behind that word: Ash-Shakur.
screen: `NOBODY SAW.` → `A THORNY BRANCH ON THE ROAD.` → `GOD THANKED HIM.`

segments.voice: Ash-Shakur comes from shukr, the word for thanks we met back at the start of the path. When a person has shukr, they're grateful. But what does it mean for God to be shakur? He doesn't need anything from us. Scholars explain it this way: God's shukr is appreciation. He notices the smallest good and rewards it far beyond its size. A branch moved, a whole life forgiven. That's the scale. The Qur'an puts it in two lines that many Muslims know by heart. In Pickthall's translation: "And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then." An atom's weight. In the Arabic it's a dharrah, a speck, some say the tiniest ant. Nothing is too small to be seen, and then answered. And the Prophet backed it up in a hadith in Sahih Muslim: don't look down on any good deed, even meeting your brother with a cheerful face. A smile is on the list. Now look back at this week, because every name has pointed here. Al-Fattah opened. Al-'Alim knew what the heart hides. As-Sami' and al-Basir heard the whisper and saw the ant. Al-Latif worked too finely to see. Al-Halim held back. Al-Wadud loved, and showed it. And Ash-Shakur notices the smallest thing you did, and doesn't let it disappear. Seven names, one picture: nothing about you is too small, too quiet, or too hidden to count.
screen: `SHUKR — THANKS, FROM GOD.` · `AN ATOM'S WEIGHT OF GOOD.` · `EVEN A CHEERFUL FACE.` · `SEVEN NAMES THIS WEEK.` · then, large: `NOTHING SMALL IS LOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank someone for something tiny. Sit, and go back over today. Find the smallest kind thing anyone did for you. The barista who remembered your name. The coworker who refilled the printer. The kid who put their plate in the sink without being asked. Choose one. Picture the moment you'll thank them, and exactly what you'll say, naming the small thing, so they know it was seen. If you pray, you can thank God for it too. The bell holds the time.
Ash-Shakur. The Appreciative: the One who notices the smallest good and rewards it far beyond its size. Today's word.
Your line: nothing small is lost. Today, thank that one person, out loud, for the tiny thing. Day two hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Many Muslims take the hadith of the thorny branch literally and clear obstacles from paths and roads, and the Prophet counted removing harm from the road as a branch of faith.

fork.reveal: the man in the hadith moved it, and God thanked him and forgave him. the smallest deed, answered at full size.

original.note: Arabic: the Appreciative. from shukr, thanks: here, the One who rewards small good richly.

trapdoor: what you thought: we're supposed to thank God.
what it means: God is the Appreciative one, who notices the smallest good and rewards it far beyond its size.
what a scholar hears: the hadith uses the verb shakara of God: he thanked the man. scholars read God's shukr as reward, never as need.

sources.quoted: And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then
